1.concept: An AVL tree is a BST that automatically re-balances itself after every insertion so that the height difference between any node's left and right subtree — its balance factor — never exceeds 1. When an insertion pushes that difference too far, the tree performs a rotation to restore balance. That constant maintenance is what guarantees O(log n) height no matter what order values are inserted in — the worst-case degeneration a plain BST is vulnerable to simply can't happen here. The cost is that every insertion may trigger a rotation, but a rotation only touches a small constant number of pointers, so it's O(1) — the balancing overhead is cheap; what you're buying is a hard guarantee instead of a hope.
1.analogy: A tightrope walker constantly making tiny weight shifts to stay centered. A plain BST can lean further and further to one side with every insert until it's basically a straight line; an AVL tree corrects its lean immediately, every time.
1.mascotDialogue: Balance factor is just left-height minus right-height. Anything outside [-1, 1] triggers a rotation before we move on. That's the whole self-balancing trick.

2.mascotDialogue: rotateRight lifts the left child up to become the new root of this subtree, and hands its old right child down to the demoted node — three pointer swaps, one operation.

3.mascotDialogue: After the rotation, 20 sits on top with balance factor 0 on both sides. Without it, 30 would've had a balance factor of 2 — a straight leaning line, not a tree anymore.

4.bugDescription: Balance factor at node 30 is 2 (left height 2, right height 0) — outside the allowed [-1, 1] range. Without the rotation, this AVL tree has degraded into what's structurally just a linked list, losing the whole point of logarithmic search time.
4.mascotDialogue: The balance factor badge on node 30 is the tell here — 2 is a hard violation, displayed plainly, not something you'd have to compute by hand to notice.

5.question: What balance factor range is allowed at every node in a valid AVL tree?
hints: Balance factor is left-height minus right-height.
Anything outside this range means a rotation is overdue.
5.solution: A valid AVL tree requires every node's balance factor to be -1, 0, or 1 — any node outside that range must trigger a rotation.
